lessons.title: Claude Code building blocks: rules, skills, commands, agents and memory
lessons.eli5: Think of Claude Code as a new teammate. Rules are the house rules pinned on the wall, skills are the how-to binders on the shelf, commands are buttons you press, subagents are specialists you can send off on an errand, and agent memory is the teammate's own notebook of things they've learned.
lessons.body:
## Five building blocks

The Developer exam guide lists Claude Code's core components as **Rules, Skills, Commands, Agents and Agent Memory**. Each one answers a different question about how you shape Claude Code's behavior. If you know what each component is for, when it loads, who writes it and where it lives, most Domain 3 questions become a matter of matching the scenario to the right block.

| Component | What it is | When it loads | Who writes it | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Rules** | Standing instructions: `CLAUDE.md` files plus `.claude/rules/*.md` | At launch (path-scoped rules load when a matching file is read) | You and your team | `./CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/rules/`, `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` … |
| **Skills** | A packaged procedure in `SKILL.md`, with optional supporting files | Only the name and description sit in context. The full body loads when it's invoked | You or your team | `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` or `~/.claude/skills/` |
| **Commands** | Things you type with `/`: built-ins (`/init`, `/compact`) and custom ones | When you type them | Built-ins ship with Claude Code. Custom ones are written by you | `.claude/commands/*.md` (now merged into skills) |
| **Agents** (subagents) | Specialized helpers with their own prompt, tools and context window | When Claude delegates or you ask for one | You or your team | `.claude/agents/*.md` or `~/.claude/agents/` |
| **Agent Memory** | Notes Claude itself writes so it learns across sessions | `MEMORY.md` index at session start, topic files on demand | **Claude** | `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/`, or a subagent's memory directory |

Hooks, settings, MCP servers and plugins round out the picture. They get their own lessons, but keep one distinction in mind: **rules, skills and memory are context**, which Claude reads and usually follows. **Hooks and permission rules are enforcement**, which Claude Code applies no matter what the model decides.

## Rules: what Claude should always know

Rules are the always-on layer. A `CLAUDE.md` at the repository root holds the build commands, coding conventions and "don't touch this folder" notes that apply to every task. When a convention only applies to certain files, a rule in `.claude/rules/` with a `paths:` glob loads only when Claude reads a matching file:

```markdown
---
paths:
  - "src/api/**/*.ts"
---
# API handlers
- Validate every request body with the shared zod schemas in src/api/schemas.
- Return errors as { error: { code, message } }.
```

Rules are delivered as context, not as a system-level guarantee. Keep each file short (the docs suggest under about 200 lines), because every always-loaded line costs tokens on every turn.

## Skills: how to do a specific job

A skill is a reusable procedure, such as "how we cut a release" or "how to write a migration". Its frontmatter `description` tells Claude when the skill is relevant. Until then, only that short listing costs context, which is called **progressive disclosure**. You can invoke a skill yourself with `/skill-name`, or Claude can pick it up when the task matches.

Use a skill instead of `CLAUDE.md` when the content is long, task-specific and not needed on most turns.

## Commands: what you trigger by hand

**Built-in commands** control the session: `/init` (create a starter `CLAUDE.md`), `/memory`, `/compact`, `/clear`, `/resume`, `/permissions`, `/model`, `/context`, `/agents` and others. **Custom commands** are your own prompts saved as files. In current Claude Code, custom commands have been merged into skills: `.claude/commands/deploy.md` and `.claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md` both create `/deploy`. The old commands folder still works, but new work should use skills because they support supporting files and extra frontmatter.

## Agents: a separate pair of hands

A subagent is a Markdown file with frontmatter (`name`, `description`, optional `tools`, `model` and more) and a system prompt in the body. When Claude delegates to it, the subagent works in its **own context window** and returns a summary. That keeps noisy exploration, long logs or big search results out of your main conversation. A subagent does **not** see your conversation history, so the delegation message has to carry whatever it needs.

Claude Code also ships built-in subagents such as **Explore** (read-only codebase search), **Plan** (used during plan mode) and **general-purpose**.

## Agent Memory: what Claude learns on its own

Rules are written by people. **Auto memory** is written by Claude. As it works, Claude saves notes such as build quirks, your corrections and project facts to `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/`. A `MEMORY.md` file there acts as the index. At the time of writing, its first 200 lines or 25KB load at the start of each session, and topic files are read on demand. Auto memory is machine-local and is not committed to git. Toggle it with `/memory` or the `autoMemoryEnabled` setting.

Subagents can have their own persistent memory too. Add `memory: user`, `memory: project` or `memory: local` to the agent's frontmatter, and it gets a directory (for example `.claude/agent-memory/<agent-name>/` for project scope) that it reads and curates across conversations.

## Worked example: where does this belong?

| Need | Component |
|---|---|
| "Always run `pnpm test`, never `npm test`" for the whole team | Project `CLAUDE.md` (rule) |
| Testing conventions for `*.test.tsx` files spread across 40 folders | `.claude/rules/testing.md` with a `paths` glob |
| A 15-step release checklist used twice a month | Skill (`.claude/skills/release/SKILL.md`) |
| A security reviewer with read-only tools and its own prompt | Subagent in `.claude/agents/` |
| Claude remembering that the staging DB needs a VPN, without anyone writing it down | Auto memory |
| "Never run `rm -rf`" as a guarantee | Not a component on this list: a permission `deny` rule or a PreToolUse hook |

## Sharing model

Anything committed in the repository (`CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/rules/`, `.claude/skills/`, `.claude/agents/`, `.claude/settings.json`) is shared with the team. Anything under `~/.claude/` is personal and follows you across projects. Auto memory is personal and stays on one machine.
keyTakeaways: The five core components are Rules (CLAUDE.md and .claude/rules), Skills (SKILL.md), Commands (built-in and custom slash commands), Agents (subagents) and Agent Memory.
Rules load at launch (or by path), skills load on demand through their description, commands run when you type them, subagents work in their own context, and auto memory is written by Claude.
Rules, skills and memory are context. Permissions and hooks are enforcement.
Custom slash commands have been merged into skills: .claude/commands/x.md and .claude/skills/x/SKILL.md both create /x.
Files committed under the repo's .claude/ (plus CLAUDE.md) are shared with the team. Files under ~/.claude/ are personal.
Subagents don't inherit your conversation history. Pass what they need in the delegation message.
examTips: Map each scenario to one component: always-needed fact → CLAUDE.md, file-type convention → path-scoped rule, on-demand procedure → skill, isolated specialist → subagent, learned-over-time notes → agent memory.
When a question says something must happen 'always' or 'guaranteed', the answer is usually a hook or permission rule, not a component that only adds context.
Watch for the word 'shared'. Shared means committed project files, never ~/.claude/.
commonTraps: Putting a long, rarely used procedure in CLAUDE.md, where it costs tokens on every turn, instead of in a skill.
Assuming auto memory is shared with teammates. It's machine-local and not in git.
Treating a subagent as if it can see the main conversation.
Believing .claude/commands/ no longer works. It still works; skills are just the preferred format.

lessons.title: The CLAUDE.md hierarchy and repository initialization with /init
lessons.eli5: CLAUDE.md is a briefing note Claude reads before it starts working. There can be several notes, from the company, from you and from the project, and Claude reads them all together. /init writes the first draft of the project's note for you.
lessons.body:
## Why a hierarchy?

Different instructions have different owners. Your company's security team, you personally, your project team and the maintainers of one subfolder all want Claude to know something, so Claude Code reads `CLAUDE.md` files from several places and **combines** them.

## The levels

| Level | Location | Who sees it | In git? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Managed policy** | OS-level path, e.g. `/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/CLAUDE.md` (macOS) or `/etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md` (Linux/WSL) | Everyone on the machine. Can't be excluded | No (deployed by IT) |
| **User** | `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` | Only you, in every project | No |
| **Project** | `./CLAUDE.md` or `./.claude/CLAUDE.md` | The whole team | **Yes** |
| **Local** | `./CLAUDE.local.md` (add to `.gitignore`) | Only you, in this project | No |
| **Subdirectory** | `packages/api/CLAUDE.md` etc. | Anyone working in that folder | Yes |

### How they combine

- Files are **concatenated, not overridden**. All applicable files go into context. If two files conflict, Claude sees both, so resolve conflicts by editing the files rather than relying on "the closer one wins".
- At launch, Claude Code walks from the filesystem root down to your current working directory and loads every `CLAUDE.md` (and `CLAUDE.local.md`) it finds on that path. Content closer to your working directory is read later.
- `CLAUDE.md` files in folders **below** your working directory load **lazily**, only when Claude reads files in those folders.
- Project-root `CLAUDE.md` is re-read from disk after `/compact`, so its instructions survive compaction. Instructions you only typed into the chat can be lost.

## Keeping it modular

Two tools stop one giant file from growing:

1. **`@imports`.** Write `@docs/testing.md` inside `CLAUDE.md` to pull another file in. Relative paths resolve from the importing file, and imports can nest up to four hops. Imports **organize** content but don't save tokens, because imported files still load at launch.
2. **`.claude/rules/`.** Each Markdown file is a rule. Without frontmatter it loads at launch like `CLAUDE.md`. With a `paths:` glob it loads only when Claude reads a matching file, which is the right tool for conventions that follow file types across many folders.

```markdown
# CLAUDE.md (project root)
## Commands
- Install: `pnpm install`
- Test one file: `pnpm vitest run <path>`
- Lint before commit: `pnpm lint --fix`

## Conventions
- TypeScript strict mode. No `any` in new code.
- See @docs/architecture.md for service boundaries.

## Don't
- Don't edit generated files in `src/gen/`.
```

## Repository initialization with /init

Run `/init` in a repository and Claude Code analyzes the codebase and writes a starter `CLAUDE.md` with the build and test commands, structure and conventions it can detect. If a `CLAUDE.md` already exists, `/init` suggests improvements instead of starting over. At the time of writing, setting `CLAUDE_CODE_NEW_INIT=1` gives an interactive flow that also walks through skills, hooks and personal memory files.

A sensible bootstrap sequence for a team repository:

1. Run `/init` and read every line it produced. Remove anything generic ("write clean code") and anything wrong.
2. Add what Claude can't infer: the exact test command, forbidden directories, review expectations.
3. Commit `CLAUDE.md` so every teammate and every CI run gets it.
4. Put personal preferences (editor habits, your sandbox URLs) in `CLAUDE.local.md` or `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, not the shared file.
5. Move long, rarely needed procedures into skills, and file-type conventions into `.claude/rules/`.

## Inspecting what loaded

- **`/memory`** lists the `CLAUDE.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md` and rules files in the session, opens them for editing, and toggles auto memory.
- **`/context`** shows what is using the context window, including the memory files.

## Diagnosing "Claude ignores our rule"

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| A new teammate's Claude doesn't follow team conventions | Conventions were written in someone's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` | Move them to project `CLAUDE.md` and commit |
| Rules for `services/payments/` never apply when you start in the repo root | Subdirectory file loads lazily | Expected. It loads once Claude reads files there. For cross-cutting rules, use root `CLAUDE.md` or a path-scoped rule |
| Test conventions apply inconsistently to scattered test files | Rules were put in several per-folder `CLAUDE.md` files | One `.claude/rules/testing.md` with `paths: ["**/*.test.*"]` |
| A rule is "mostly" followed but must be absolute | `CLAUDE.md` is guidance, not enforcement | Add a permission deny rule or a hook |
| Context feels crowded every turn | `CLAUDE.md` has grown to hundreds of lines | Trim, move procedures to skills, and scope rules by path |

## CLAUDE.md vs auto memory

Both carry knowledge across sessions, but they differ in authorship and sharing. `CLAUDE.md` is **written by humans** and can be committed for the team. Auto memory is **written by Claude**, stored per project under `~/.claude/projects/`, and stays on one machine. If a learned fact should apply to the whole team, promote it from memory into `CLAUDE.md`.
keyTakeaways: Levels: managed policy, user (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md), project (./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md), local (CLAUDE.local.md) and subdirectory files.
All applicable files are concatenated, not overridden. Ancestor files load at launch, and subdirectory files below the working directory load lazily.
@imports organize content but don't save tokens. Path-scoped .claude/rules/ files load only when matching files are read.
/init analyzes the repo and writes a starter CLAUDE.md, or suggests improvements if one exists. Review and trim what it writes.
/memory shows and edits loaded instruction files and toggles auto memory. /context shows what fills the window.
Project-root CLAUDE.md is re-read after /compact, so standing instructions survive compaction.
examTips: 'New teammate doesn't get the convention' → it was in user-level CLAUDE.md; move it to the committed project file.
'Conventions for test files scattered across folders' → .claude/rules/ with a paths glob, not per-folder CLAUDE.md files.
'Bootstrap a repo for Claude Code' → /init, then edit and commit the result.
commonTraps: Thinking the closest CLAUDE.md overrides the others. They are combined, so conflicts must be fixed in the files.
Expecting @imports to reduce context usage.
Committing CLAUDE.local.md, which is meant to be personal and git-ignored.
Accepting /init output unedited, generic advice included.

lessons.title: settings.json configuration: scopes, precedence and permissions
lessons.eli5: If CLAUDE.md is the briefing, settings.json is the building's security system: which doors open on their own, which ones need a badge and which ones stay locked. The company's rules beat the team's rules, and the team's rules beat your personal ones.
lessons.body:
## What settings.json controls

`CLAUDE.md` tells Claude what to know. **`settings.json` tells Claude Code how to behave.** Settings cover permissions, the default model, environment variables, hooks, the default permission mode, transcript retention and more. Unlike `CLAUDE.md`, Claude Code enforces settings itself. The model can't talk its way past a deny rule.

## The scopes and their precedence

| Precedence | Scope | File | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (highest) | **Managed** | `managed-settings.json` in a system directory, delivered by MDM, or server-managed from the admin console | Org policy that users can't override |
| 2 | **Command line** | Flags such as `--model`, `--permission-mode`, `--settings <file-or-json>` | One session or one CI run |
| 3 | **Local project** | `.claude/settings.local.json` | Your personal tweaks for this repo (git-ignored) |
| 4 | **Shared project** | `.claude/settings.json` | Team defaults, committed |
| 5 (lowest) | **User** | `~/.claude/settings.json` | Your defaults in every project |

Memorize the order **managed > CLI > local > project > user**. When the same scalar key (for example `model`) is set in two places, the higher scope wins.

**List-valued keys merge.** `permissions.allow` entries from user, project and local settings are combined rather than replaced. That's why a teammate's personal allow rule can sit alongside the team's list.

## A team settings file

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/claude-code-settings.json",
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(pnpm test *)",
      "Bash(pnpm lint *)",
      "Bash(git diff *)"
    ],
    "ask": ["Bash(git push *)"],
    "deny": [
      "Read(./.env)",
      "Read(./secrets/**)",
      "Bash(curl *)"
    ],
    "defaultMode": "acceptEdits"
  },
  "env": {
    "NODE_ENV": "development"
  }
}
```

Commit this as `.claude/settings.json` and every collaborator starts with the same guardrails. Personal additions go in `.claude/settings.local.json`, which Claude Code adds to git excludes when it creates the file.

## Permission rules in one minute

- Rule syntax is `Tool` or `Tool(specifier)`: `Bash(npm run *)`, `Read(./src/**)`, `Edit(/docs/**)`, `WebFetch(domain:example.com)`, `mcp__github__*`.
- Evaluation order is **deny, then ask, then allow, and the first match wins.** Specificity doesn't matter, so a broad `deny` beats a narrow `allow`.
- A trailing space plus `*` gives a prefix match. `Bash(git diff *)` matches `git diff --stat` but not `git diff-index`.
- Deny rules apply in **every** permission mode, including `bypassPermissions`.
- `/permissions` shows each rule and which settings file it came from.

## Other keys worth knowing

| Key | What it does |
|---|---|
| `model` | Default model for sessions |
| `env` | Environment variables applied to each session |
| `hooks` | Lifecycle hooks (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop …) for deterministic actions |
| `permissions.defaultMode` | Starting permission mode (`default`, `acceptEdits`, `plan`, `auto`, `dontAsk`, `bypassPermissions`) |
| `permissions.additionalDirectories` | Extra directories Claude may access |
| `cleanupPeriodDays` | How long local session transcripts are kept (30 days by default at the time of writing) |
| `autoMemoryEnabled` | Turn auto memory on or off |
| `disableAutoMode` (managed) | Set to `"disable"` to remove auto mode for the organization |

## Settings vs CLAUDE.md vs MCP config

These are easy to mix up:

| You want to … | Put it in |
|---|---|
| Teach conventions and commands | `CLAUDE.md` |
| Allow, ask or deny tools, set the mode, add hooks or env vars | `settings.json` |
| Share an MCP server with the team | `.mcp.json` at the repo root (project scope) |
| Keep a personal MCP server | `claude mcp add` with local or user scope (stored in `~/.claude.json`, not `settings.local.json`) |

## Worked example: why did my allow rule not work?

A developer adds `"allow": ["Bash(git push *)"]` to `.claude/settings.local.json`, but Claude still asks before pushing. The team's `.claude/settings.json` contains `"ask": ["Bash(git push *)"]`. Since **ask is evaluated before allow**, the ask rule matches first. Precedence of files doesn't help here: rules from all scopes are merged and then evaluated deny → ask → allow. The fix is a conversation with the team about removing the ask rule, not a more specific allow.

## Managed settings for organizations

Admins use managed settings to enforce policy that no user or project can override: deny rules for sensitive paths, disabling `bypassPermissions` mode, turning off auto mode, allow-listing plugin marketplaces, or forcing an org-wide `CLAUDE.md`. If an exam scenario says "must apply to every developer and nobody should be able to change it", managed settings is the answer.
keyTakeaways: Scopes, highest first: managed > command line > local (.claude/settings.local.json) > project (.claude/settings.json) > user (~/.claude/settings.json).
Scalar keys take the highest scope's value. List keys such as permissions.allow merge across scopes.
Permission rules are evaluated deny → ask → allow, and the first match wins regardless of specificity.
Deny rules apply in every permission mode, including bypassPermissions.
Settings are enforced by Claude Code. CLAUDE.md can't grant or revoke permissions.
Shared MCP servers belong in .mcp.json. Personal or local MCP config lives in ~/.claude.json, not settings.local.json.
examTips: 'Must apply to every developer and can't be overridden' → managed settings.
'Team-wide default, committed' → .claude/settings.json. 'Just me in this repo' → .claude/settings.local.json.
If an allow rule 'doesn't work', look for a matching ask or deny rule anywhere in the merged settings.
commonTraps: Thinking a more specific allow rule beats a broader deny rule.
Assuming local settings override project ask or deny rules. Rule lists merge and are evaluated by type.
Using CLAUDE.md text like 'never read .env' instead of a Read deny rule.
Writing Bash(git diff*) without a space, which also matches git diff-index.

lessons.title: Slash commands, skills and subagents in practice
lessons.eli5: Built-in slash commands are the remote control's standard buttons. Skills are recipes you write once and call by name. Subagents are helpers you send into another room so the mess they make while working stays out of your conversation.
lessons.body:
## Built-in slash commands you should recognize

Type `/` in a session to see every command. The exam won't ask for the full list, but it does expect you to pick the right command for a situation.

| Command | Use it to … |
|---|---|
| `/init` | Generate a starter `CLAUDE.md` for the repository |
| `/memory` | Edit `CLAUDE.md` files, view auto memory entries, toggle auto memory |
| `/compact [focus]` | Summarize the conversation to free context and keep going |
| `/clear` | Start a new, empty conversation (the old one stays resumable) |
| `/resume [name]` | Switch to an earlier session, or open the picker |
| `/rename <name>` | Name the current session so you can resume it by name |
| `/branch [name]` | Fork the conversation to try a different approach |
| `/rewind` | Roll back the conversation and/or code to a checkpoint |
| `/context` | See what is consuming the context window |
| `/permissions` | View and edit allow, ask and deny rules |
| `/model` | Switch model (and adjust effort where supported) |
| `/plan [task]` | Enter plan mode for read-only analysis before edits |
| `/hooks` | View configured hooks |
| `/skills` | List available skills |
| `/mcp` | Manage MCP server connections |
| `/usage` | Session cost and plan usage (`/cost` is an alias) |

Some entries in the `/` menu, such as `/simplify` and `/batch`, are **bundled skills**: prompts that ship with Claude Code and behave like skills you write yourself.

## Custom commands are skills now

Historically, a custom command was a Markdown file in `.claude/commands/`. Claude Code has merged commands into skills, so these two files both create `/review-pr`:

```text
.claude/commands/review-pr.md
.claude/skills/review-pr/SKILL.md
```

The old location still works, but a skill directory can also hold supporting files (templates, scripts, reference docs) and accepts richer frontmatter. Where the file lives decides who gets it:

| Location | Scope |
|---|---|
| `.claude/skills/` or `.claude/commands/` in the repo | Shared with everyone who clones it |
| `~/.claude/skills/` or `~/.claude/commands/` | Personal, available in all your projects |
| A plugin | Namespaced, e.g. `/my-plugin:review-pr` |

## Anatomy of a skill

```markdown
---
name: review-pr
description: Review the current branch's diff against our checklist. Use when asked to review a PR or a diff.
argument-hint: "[pr-number]"
allowed-tools: Bash(git diff *) Bash(gh pr view *)
---
Review PR $ARGUMENTS.

1. Run `git diff origin/main...HEAD`.
2. Check each item in [checklist.md](checklist.md).
3. Report findings as a table: file, line, severity, fix.
```

Key fields:

- **`description`**: tells Claude when to use the skill. Only names and descriptions sit in context until the skill runs, so write this line carefully.
- **`$ARGUMENTS`**: replaced with whatever follows `/review-pr` (`$0`, `$1` … for positional arguments).
- **`allowed-tools`**: pre-approves those tools while the skill runs. It's a convenience grant, not a sandbox.
- **`disable-model-invocation: true`**: only you can trigger it. Use this for side-effect workflows like deploys.
- **`context: fork`**: runs the skill in an isolated subagent so its verbose output stays out of your main conversation.

Keep `SKILL.md` focused (the docs suggest under about 500 lines) and push detail into supporting files that load only when needed.

## Subagents in practice

```markdown
---
name: test-runner
description: Runs the test suite and diagnoses failures. Use after code changes.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
model: sonnet
memory: project
---
You run tests and explain failures. Report the failing test, the root
cause and a minimal fix. Never modify test expectations to make them pass.
```

- `name` and `description` are required. `description` drives automatic delegation.
- `tools` is an allowlist. If you omit it, the subagent inherits all tools. Least privilege means listing only what it needs.
- `model` can pick a cheaper or stronger model per agent, or `inherit`.
- `memory` (`user`, `project` or `local`) gives the agent a persistent memory directory. It reads the first part of its own `MEMORY.md` at startup and curates it over time.
- The subagent starts with a **fresh context**: its own system prompt, the task message and the project's `CLAUDE.md`, but **not** your conversation history. Put needed findings in the delegation prompt.

Project agents live in `.claude/agents/` (shared). Personal agents live in `~/.claude/agents/`. Edit the files directly or ask Claude to create one.

## Choosing between them

| Situation | Best fit | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A fixed procedure you trigger by hand ("deploy to staging") | Skill with `disable-model-invocation: true` | You decide when side effects happen |
| Know-how Claude should apply when relevant ("how we write migrations") | Skill with a clear `description` | Loads on demand and saves context |
| Exploring 200 files to find every caller of an API | Subagent (or Explore) | Keeps noisy output out of the main context |
| A reviewer that must not edit files | Subagent with `tools: Read, Grep, Glob` | The tool allowlist enforces read-only |
| A fact every task needs | `CLAUDE.md` | Always loaded |

## Worked example: sharing a team command

Your team wants everyone to have `/changelog`, which drafts release notes from merged PRs. Create `.claude/skills/changelog/SKILL.md` (or `.claude/commands/changelog.md`), commit it, and every clone gets the command. Putting it in `~/.claude/` would only give it to you. Describing it in `CLAUDE.md` wouldn't create a command at all.
keyTakeaways: Know the built-ins by purpose: /init, /memory, /compact, /clear, /resume, /rename, /branch, /rewind, /context, /permissions, /model, /plan, /hooks, /skills, /mcp, /usage.
Custom commands and skills share the /name namespace. Project location means shared, ~/.claude location means personal.
A skill's description decides when Claude uses it. Only names and descriptions sit in context until a skill is invoked.
disable-model-invocation: true makes a skill manual-only. context: fork runs it in an isolated subagent. allowed-tools pre-approves tools while it runs.
Subagent frontmatter: name and description are required. tools is an allowlist (omit it to inherit all), and model and memory are optional.
Subagents return a summary to the main conversation, which keeps their exploration out of it.
examTips: 'Team-shared /command' → commit it under .claude/skills/ or .claude/commands/ in the repo.
'Helper must be read-only' → a subagent with a restricted tools list, not a CLAUDE.md instruction.
'Keep verbose exploration out of the main context' → a subagent or a skill with context: fork.
commonTraps: Defining a command inside CLAUDE.md. That's text, not a command.
Assuming allowed-tools in a skill is a security sandbox. It's a pre-approval convenience.
Writing a vague skill description, so Claude never picks the skill up.
Omitting tools on a subagent meant to be restricted. It then inherits everything.

lessons.title: Session management and permission modes, including auto mode
lessons.eli5: A session is a saved conversation you can pause and pick up later, like a bookmarked chat. Permission modes are how much freedom you give Claude. In auto mode, a second AI acts as a safety guard and checks each action before it happens.
lessons.body:
## Sessions: saved conversations you can return to

A **session** is a conversation tied to a project directory. Claude Code saves it continuously as a JSONL transcript under `~/.claude/projects/<project>/`, so you can leave and come back. Transcripts are cleaned up after 30 days by default at the time of writing, which you can change with `cleanupPeriodDays`.

| You want to … | Use |
|---|---|
| Reopen the most recent conversation in this directory | `claude --continue` (`-c`) |
| Pick from a list of earlier sessions | `claude --resume` (`-r`) or `/resume` inside a session |
| Resume a specific session | `claude --resume <name-or-session-id>` |
| Name a session | `claude -n auth-refactor` at startup, or `/rename auth-refactor` |
| Try a different approach without losing the original | `/branch [name]`, or `claude --continue --fork-session` |
| Free context but keep going | `/compact [focus instructions]` |
| Start fresh in the same terminal | `/clear` (the previous conversation stays resumable) |
| Roll back code and/or conversation | `/rewind` (or Esc twice) |

A resumed session restores the full history, including tool calls, and in most cases the model. Settings files are re-read at launch. One-off flags such as `--mcp-config` or `--add-dir` must be passed again.

### Compact or clear?

- **`/compact`** replaces older history with a summary in the **same** conversation. Project-root `CLAUDE.md` is re-read from disk, so standing instructions survive, but details you only said in chat may be lost.
- **`/clear`** starts a **new** conversation with an empty context. Use it when you switch to an unrelated task, so stale context doesn't steer the new one.

Session hygiene is tested: one session per task, `/clear` between unrelated tasks, `/compact` when a long task fills the window, and named sessions when you juggle parallel work.

### Checkpoints aren't git

Each prompt creates a checkpoint that `/rewind` can restore. Checkpoints don't track changes made through Bash (`rm`, `mv`, scripts), edits made outside Claude Code, or most subagent edits. Use git for real version control.

## Permission modes: how much Claude may do unasked

A permission mode sets the baseline for what runs without a prompt. Switch with **Shift+Tab**, `--permission-mode <mode>`, or `permissions.defaultMode` in settings.

| Mode | Runs without asking | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| `default` (shown as Manual) | Reads only | Sensitive work, reviewing every action |
| `acceptEdits` | Reads, file edits and common filesystem commands (`mkdir`, `mv`, `cp` …) | Iterating on code you're watching |
| `plan` | Read-only exploration, then a written plan. No source edits until you approve | Large, multi-file or ambiguous changes |
| `auto` | Most actions, after a **classifier model** reviews each one | Hands-off work where you trust the direction |
| `dontAsk` | Only pre-approved tools. Anything that would prompt is denied | Locked-down CI |
| `bypassPermissions` | Everything except deny rules and a few protected checks | Isolated containers or VMs only |

### Auto mode in detail

In auto mode, a separate classifier model reviews actions before they run, instead of you. It blocks actions that escalate beyond your request, target unrecognized infrastructure, or look driven by hostile content Claude read (prompt injection). Facts to know, at the time of writing:

- With recent Claude Code versions, auto mode is the **built-in starting mode** for interactive terminal and VS Code sessions, unless settings choose another mode.
- It requires a supported model. Older models such as Haiku and claude-3 models aren't supported.
- Explicit `ask` rules still force a prompt, and `deny` rules still block.
- If the classifier blocks actions **3 times in a row or 20 times in total**, auto mode pauses and Claude Code falls back to prompting you.
- Admins can remove it with `permissions.disableAutoMode: "disable"` in managed settings.
- The docs warn that auto mode **reduces prompts but doesn't guarantee safety**. It's not a substitute for reviewing sensitive operations.

### Plan mode workflow

Enter with Shift+Tab, `/plan fix the auth bug`, or `claude --permission-mode plan`. Claude explores and writes a plan. You can then approve it (optionally switching to auto mode or auto-accept edits), edit it with Ctrl+G, or keep planning. Use plan mode for architectural or multi-file changes. Use direct execution for a clear, single-file fix.

## Worked example: a long refactor across two days

1. Day 1: `claude -n payments-refactor`, then `/plan migrate payments to the new client`. Review and approve the plan.
2. Work in `acceptEdits` while you watch the diffs. When the context fills, run `/compact focus on remaining migration steps`.
3. Day 2: `claude --resume payments-refactor`. History, model and mode come back.
4. To test a risky alternative, run `/branch try-adapter-pattern`. The original line of work stays intact.
5. Starting an unrelated bug fix? Run `/clear` (or open a new session) rather than reusing the refactor conversation.
keyTakeaways: --continue reopens the latest session, --resume opens the picker or a named/ID session, /rename and -n name sessions, and /branch or --fork-session forks one.
/compact summarizes and continues the same conversation. /clear starts a new, empty one (the old one stays resumable).
Checkpoints (/rewind) don't track Bash-driven file changes and are not a substitute for git.
Modes: default (Manual), acceptEdits, plan, auto, dontAsk, bypassPermissions. Switch with Shift+Tab, --permission-mode or permissions.defaultMode.
Auto mode: a classifier model reviews actions. Ask and deny rules still apply. Repeated blocks (3 in a row or 20 total) fall back to prompting. Admins can disable it.
bypassPermissions is for isolated containers or VMs only.
examTips: 'Reduce prompts but keep a safety check' → auto mode. 'No prompts in an isolated throwaway container' → bypassPermissions.
'Analyze before editing a large change' → plan mode. 'Small, clear fix' → direct execution.
'Continue yesterday's task by name' → claude --resume <name>.
commonTraps: Using /clear when the goal is to keep working on the same task with less context. That's /compact.
Believing auto mode guarantees safety, or that it overrides deny rules.
Expecting /rewind to undo files deleted with rm.
Reusing one long session for unrelated tasks, which lets stale context steer new work.

lessons.title: Headless mode, output formats and streaming
lessons.eli5: Headless mode is like leaving Claude a written task and walking away: it does the job and leaves the answer on your desk without asking you anything. Streaming mode is watching the answer appear word by word instead of waiting for the finished page.
lessons.body:
## Interactive vs headless

Interactive Claude Code is a chat in your terminal. **Headless mode** runs one prompt non-interactively and exits, which is what scripts, cron jobs and CI pipelines need. Turn it on with `-p` (long form `--print`):

```bash
claude -p "Summarize the changes in this branch" --allowedTools "Bash(git diff *),Read"
```

Claude Code exits with code `0` on success and non-zero on failure, so a script can branch on the result. A pipeline that hangs waiting for input almost always means `-p` was left off. Made-up options such as a "headless" environment variable or a `--batch` flag don't exist.

Headless runs read stdin, so you can pipe data in (at the time of writing, piped input is capped at 10MB):

```bash
cat build-error.log | claude -p "Explain the root cause in three bullets" > diagnosis.md
```

## Output formats

| `--output-format` | You get | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| `text` (default) | Plain response text | A human reads it, or you write it to a file |
| `json` | One JSON object: `result`, `session_id`, usage and cost metadata | A script needs the answer plus metadata |
| `stream-json` | Newline-delimited JSON events as they happen | You want progress or tokens in real time |

### Structured results with a schema

Add `--json-schema` to `--output-format json` and the validated object arrives in a **`structured_output`** field:

```bash
claude -p "List every TODO in src/ with file and line" \
  --output-format json \
  --json-schema '{"type":"object","properties":{"todos":{"type":"array","items":{"type":"object","properties":{"file":{"type":"string"},"line":{"type":"integer"},"text":{"type":"string"}},"required":["file","line","text"]}}},"required":["todos"]}' \
  | jq '.structured_output.todos'
```

An invalid schema makes the command fail with an error rather than silently returning text.

## Streaming mode

`stream-json` emits one JSON object per line while the run is in progress. To get **token-level** deltas, combine it with `--verbose` and `--include-partial-messages`:

```bash
claude -p "Draft a migration plan" \
  --output-format stream-json --verbose --include-partial-messages \
  | jq -rj 'select(.type=="stream_event" and .event.delta.type?=="text_delta") | .event.delta.text'
```

What you'll see in the stream:

- A `system` / `init` event near the start with the model, tools, MCP servers and plugins. CI can fail fast if a required MCP server didn't load.
- Assistant and user messages, including tool calls. Subagent messages carry a `parent_tool_use_id`.
- `system` / `api_retry` events when Claude Code retries a failed API call.
- A final `result` message with the response text, cost and session metadata.

Pick streaming when someone or something is watching progress: a dashboard, a chat bridge, or a long CI job whose logs should update live. Pick `json` when you only need the final answer.

## Continuing a headless conversation

```bash
sid=$(claude -p "Review src/billing for N+1 queries" --output-format json | jq -r '.session_id')
claude -p "Now propose fixes for the top three" --resume "$sid"
```

`--continue` resumes the most recent conversation. `--resume <session-id>` targets a specific one, which is safer when several jobs run in parallel.

## Permissions without a human

Nobody is there to click "allow" in a headless run, so decide up front:

| Need | Option |
|---|---|
| Pre-approve specific tools | `--allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash(pnpm test *)"` |
| Block specific tools | `--disallowedTools` |
| Accept file edits as a baseline | `--permission-mode acceptEdits` |
| Deny anything not pre-approved | `--permission-mode dontAsk` |
| Let the classifier decide | `--permission-mode auto` |
| Make sure nothing waits on a prompt | `--permission-prompts none` (recent versions) |

## Reproducible runs with --bare

Without extra flags, `claude -p` loads the same context as an interactive session: hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers from `.mcp.json`, auto memory and `CLAUDE.md`. `--bare` skips all of that auto-discovery, so a run behaves the same on every machine. You pass in what you need (`--append-system-prompt`, `--settings`, `--mcp-config`, `--agents`). Bare mode authenticates with `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (or an `apiKeyHelper`) rather than your subscription login. The docs recommend it for scripted calls and say it will become the `-p` default.

## Other useful flags

- `--append-system-prompt "…"` adds instructions while keeping Claude Code's defaults. `--system-prompt` replaces them.
- `--max-turns N` caps the agentic loop in automation.
- `--model` pins the model for the run.
- Custom skills work headless: put `/skill-name` in the prompt string.

## Headless vs the Agent SDK

`claude -p` is the CLI face of the **Claude Agent SDK**, which has the same loop, tools and context management. When you need callbacks, typed message objects or approval logic inside your own Python or TypeScript application, use the SDK packages. For shell scripts and CI steps, `claude -p` is enough.
keyTakeaways: claude -p (--print) runs one prompt non-interactively and exits: 0 on success, non-zero on failure.
--output-format: text (default), json (result, session_id, usage and cost), stream-json (newline-delimited events).
Token-level streaming needs stream-json with --verbose and --include-partial-messages.
--json-schema with --output-format json puts the validated object in structured_output.
Resume headless runs with --continue or --resume <session_id> captured from JSON output.
--bare skips auto-discovered hooks, skills, plugins, MCP, auto memory and CLAUDE.md for reproducible scripted runs, and uses ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.
examTips: 'Pipeline hangs waiting for input' → claude -p. Invented flags and environment variables are distractors.
'Need cost or session ID in a script' → --output-format json. 'Need live progress' → stream-json.
'Must parse findings reliably' → --json-schema and read structured_output.
commonTraps: Using stream-json without --verbose.
Expecting json output to stream incrementally. It arrives once, at the end.
Assuming -p runs without any project config. Without --bare it still loads hooks, .mcp.json and CLAUDE.md.
Using --continue when several jobs run in parallel. Capture and pass the session ID instead.

lessons.title: Claude Code in CI and codebase modernization
lessons.eli5: Putting Claude Code in CI is like hiring a careful night-shift assistant: it follows the written checklist, can only touch the tools you hand it, and leaves a report for the day team to approve. For big rewrites, it works one room at a time and checks the lights still work after each room.
lessons.body:
## Claude Code in a pipeline

Teams usually bring Claude Code into CI in one of two ways:

1. **A script step** that calls `claude -p` directly. You control the prompt, flags and output parsing.
2. **The official GitHub Action** (`anthropics/claude-code-action@v1`). It wraps the same engine, responds to `@claude` mentions in issues and PRs, or runs a fixed `prompt` on any workflow event, including a schedule.

Both read the repository's `CLAUDE.md`, so the review standards, test commands and conventions you commit there shape what Claude does in CI.

### A review step with machine-readable output

```yaml
- name: Claude review
  env:
    ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
  run: |
    git diff origin/main...HEAD > diff.patch
    claude --bare -p "Review diff.patch against the checklist in CLAUDE.md. Report only new issues." \
      --append-system-prompt-file CLAUDE.md \
      --allowedTools "Read" \
      --max-turns 5 \
      --output-format json \
      --json-schema "$(cat .github/review-schema.json)" \
      > review.json
    jq '.structured_output.findings' review.json
```

What each choice buys you:

| Choice | Why |
|---|---|
| `-p` | Non-interactive, so the job can't hang on a prompt |
| `--bare` plus explicit context | Same behavior on every runner. No surprise hooks or MCP servers from a developer's setup |
| `--allowedTools "Read"` | Least privilege: the reviewer reads but can't edit or run commands |
| `--max-turns` | Bounds cost and runtime |
| `--output-format json` + `--json-schema` | Findings arrive in `structured_output` and can be posted as inline comments |
| Secrets in the CI secret store | Never commit API keys |

### Review design that people trust

- **Use an independent reviewer.** A fresh instance reviewing a diff catches more than the same session that wrote the code, which carries its own reasoning forward.
- **Give it prior findings** on re-runs and ask only for new or unresolved issues, so the PR isn't flooded with duplicates.
- **Give it existing tests** when generating tests, so it doesn't propose ones you already have.
- **Write criteria into `CLAUDE.md`** (severity levels, what to ignore, fixtures to use) rather than repeating them in every prompt.

### Permission posture in CI

Pick the narrowest posture that lets the job finish: pre-approved tools with `--allowedTools`, `dontAsk` to deny anything else, or `acceptEdits` for a job that must change files. `bypassPermissions` belongs only in a disposable, isolated container. Deny rules still apply in every mode, and hooks configured in project settings still run unless you use `--bare`.

### Hooks as CI-grade guarantees

When something must happen every time, such as running the formatter after each edit or blocking writes to `migrations/`, configure a hook in `.claude/settings.json`. A PostToolUse hook on `Edit|Write` can run the formatter. A PreToolUse hook that exits with code **2** blocks a tool call and feeds its stderr back to Claude. Exit code 1 doesn't block. Prompts and `CLAUDE.md` are guidance. Hooks are deterministic.

## Codebase modernization with Claude Code

Large upgrades, such as a framework major version, callbacks to async/await, or JavaScript to TypeScript, fail when attempted in one giant leap. A safer loop:

1. **Record the target** in `CLAUDE.md`: the conventions the new code should follow, the commands to verify it, and what's off limits.
2. **Plan first.** Start in plan mode (`/plan` or Shift+Tab). Let Claude, or an Explore subagent, map the affected files and propose an order. Review and edit the plan.
3. **Make tests the safety net.** If coverage is thin around the code being changed, add characterization tests first so behavior changes become visible.
4. **Move in small, verified steps.** Do one module or one pattern at a time. Run the tests after each step and commit each green step to git. Checkpoints don't replace commits.
5. **Isolate noisy work.** Use subagents for wide searches, and `/compact` or a fresh session between phases to keep context clean.
6. **Parallelize carefully.** Independent modules can go to separate worktrees (`claude --worktree <name>`) or background subagents. Interdependent changes stay sequential.
7. **Review like any other change.** Open PRs per step, run the Claude review job, and have a human sign off.

### Small- vs large-scale refactoring

| Scale | Approach |
|---|---|
| Rename a function used in three files | Direct execution in `acceptEdits`, then run the tests |
| Extract a service from a module | Plan mode, then step-by-step execution with tests |
| Upgrade a framework across 300 files | Plan mode, a written migration plan in the repo, batched steps, CI review on each PR, possibly parallel worktrees |

## Worked example: a nightly dependency-upgrade bot

A scheduled workflow runs `claude -p "Update minor versions in package.json, run pnpm test, and summarize breaking changes"` with `--permission-mode acceptEdits`, `--allowedTools "Bash(pnpm *)"`, `--max-turns 15` and `--output-format json`. A later step opens a PR only if the tests passed. Humans review the PR in the morning. Claude does the repetitive work, CI enforces correctness, and people keep the merge decision.
keyTakeaways: CI options: a claude -p script step, or the anthropics/claude-code-action GitHub Action (@claude mentions or a fixed prompt).
Committed CLAUDE.md carries review criteria, test commands and conventions into CI.
Use least privilege (--allowedTools, dontAsk), --max-turns, JSON schema output, and secrets in the CI secret store.
An independent reviewer instance beats self-review. Pass prior findings to avoid duplicate comments.
Hooks give deterministic guarantees. Exit code 2 from a PreToolUse hook blocks the call; exit code 1 doesn't.
Modernize with plan mode, tests as a safety net, small verified steps, a commit per green step, and subagents or worktrees for isolation.
examTips: 'Big multi-file migration' → plan mode first, then incremental execution with tests.
'Review comments keep repeating on re-runs' → include prior findings and ask only for new issues.
'Something must always run after edits' → PostToolUse hook, not a CLAUDE.md reminder.
commonTraps: Running bypassPermissions on a shared CI runner.
Having the same session that wrote the code review it.
Doing a whole-codebase rewrite in one step without tests.
Relying on checkpoints instead of git commits.

lessons.title: Claude Code quick check: scenario drill
lessons.eli5: This is a practice round. Read a short story about a team using Claude Code, then pick the right tool, file or setting. Most questions come down to 'which thing, and where does it live?'
lessons.body:
## How Domain 3 shows up on the exam

Claude Code is only about 3% of the Developer exam, so expect one or two items. They tend to be fast, factual scenario questions where knowing the exact mechanism wins: which file, which scope, which flag, which mode. The same ideas come back in Domain 2 (configuration management and application design), so this drill pays off twice.

## The four-question elimination funnel

For each option, ask:

1. **Does this mechanism exist?** Invented flags, environment variables and config files are common distractors. If you've never seen it in the docs, be suspicious.
2. **Is it the right *kind* of thing?** Context (`CLAUDE.md`, rules, skills, memory) vs enforcement (permissions, hooks) vs execution (`-p`, modes).
3. **Is it the right *scope*?** Team-shared means committed project files. Personal means `~/.claude/` or `*.local.*`. Org-wide and unchangeable means managed settings.
4. **Is it proportionate?** Prefer the built-in feature over a custom wrapper script.

## Quick-reference: scenario → answer

| Scenario signal | Answer |
|---|---|
| "Every teammate should get this instruction" | Project `CLAUDE.md`, committed |
| "Only on my machine, only this repo" | `CLAUDE.local.md` or `.claude/settings.local.json` |
| "Conventions for a file type scattered across many folders" | `.claude/rules/*.md` with a `paths:` glob |
| "Set up a new repo for Claude" | `/init` |
| "See which instruction files loaded" | `/memory` (or `/context`) |
| "Reusable workflow you trigger with `/name`, shared by the team" | `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` (or `.claude/commands/<name>.md`) |
| "Specialist with its own tools and isolated context" | Subagent in `.claude/agents/` |
| "Claude should remember lessons across sessions without anyone writing them" | Auto memory (or a subagent's `memory` field) |
| "Pipeline hangs waiting for input" | `claude -p` |
| "Script needs the session ID and cost" | `--output-format json` |
| "Live progress / token-by-token output" | `--output-format stream-json --verbose --include-partial-messages` |
| "Output must match a schema" | `--output-format json --json-schema …` → `structured_output` |
| "Fewer prompts, but something should still vet risky actions" | Auto mode (classifier) |
| "Read-only analysis before a big change" | Plan mode |
| "CI must never stop for approval" | `dontAsk` or pre-approved `--allowedTools` |
| "Pick up yesterday's work" | `claude --continue` / `claude --resume <name>` |
| "Context is full but the task continues" | `/compact` |
| "Switching to an unrelated task" | `/clear` or a new session |
| "Must be enforced, not just suggested" | Permission deny rule or hook |
| "Policy nobody can override" | Managed settings |

## Practice scenarios

Try each one before reading the answer.

### Scenario 1: The silent pipeline

A nightly job runs `claude "generate release notes from merged PRs"` and times out every night without output.

**Answer:** Add `-p` so the run is non-interactive. Add `--output-format json` if a later step parses the result, and pre-approve the tools it needs so no prompt can block it.
**Why not the others:** A longer timeout doesn't help, because the process is waiting for a human. Redirecting stdin from `/dev/null` doesn't switch Claude Code into print mode.

### Scenario 2: Two developers, two behaviors

Priya's Claude Code always uses the team's error-handling pattern. Marco's, on a fresh clone, doesn't. Priya wrote the pattern in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`.

**Answer:** Move the pattern to the project's `CLAUDE.md` (or a `.claude/rules/` file) and commit it.
**Why:** User-level files never reach version control, so only Priya ever had the instruction.

### Scenario 3: The allow rule that does nothing

A developer adds `Bash(npm publish *)` to their local `allow` list, but Claude still prompts. Project settings contain `ask: ["Bash(npm publish *)"]`.

**Answer:** Expected behavior. Rules are evaluated deny → ask → allow, and the first match wins, so the ask rule matches first.
**Trap:** Thinking that local settings outrank project settings for *rules*. File precedence matters for scalar keys. Permission lists merge and are then evaluated by type.

### Scenario 4: A reviewer that must not edit

The team wants a security-review helper that can read code but must never change it, and its long analysis shouldn't clutter the main conversation.

**Answer:** A subagent in `.claude/agents/security-reviewer.md` with `tools: Read, Grep, Glob`.
**Why:** The tool allowlist enforces read-only access, and the subagent's separate context keeps the analysis out of the main thread. A `CLAUDE.md` note saying "don't edit during reviews" is only guidance.

### Scenario 5: Fewer prompts, still guarded

A developer is tired of approving routine commands but doesn't want Claude pushing secrets or deleting infrastructure unchecked.

**Answer:** Auto mode. A classifier reviews each action and blocks risky or out-of-scope ones. Explicit `ask` and `deny` rules still apply.
**Wrong instinct:** `bypassPermissions`, which is meant for isolated containers and VMs only and removes the safety review.

### Scenario 6: Live progress in a dashboard

An internal tool shells out to Claude Code and must show text as it's generated.

**Answer:** `claude -p … --output-format stream-json --verbose --include-partial-messages`, then read `text_delta` events line by line.
**Trap:** `--output-format json` returns only once, at the end.

## Last-minute checklist

- Precedence: managed > CLI > local > project > user. Lists merge.
- Permission rules: deny → ask → allow, first match wins.
- `CLAUDE.md` files concatenate. Subdirectory files load lazily. Imports don't save tokens.
- Skills load on demand through their `description`. Custom commands are merged into skills.
- Subagents don't see your conversation history.
- `-p` for headless. `json` for metadata, `stream-json` for live events, `--json-schema` for `structured_output`.
- Auto mode means a classifier reviews actions. It reduces prompts but doesn't guarantee safety.
keyTakeaways: Check that a mechanism exists before weighing it. Invented flags and files are common distractors.
Classify the need: context (CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, memory), enforcement (permissions, hooks) or execution (-p, modes, sessions).
Match the scope: committed project files for the team, ~/.claude or *.local for one person, managed settings for the org.
Remember the orders: managed > CLI > local > project > user, and deny → ask → allow.
examTips: Expect one or two quick items. Don't overthink them, but read scope words ('team', 'only me', 'nobody can change') carefully.
Domain 2 configuration questions reuse these facts, so this drill counts there too.
commonTraps: Choosing bypassPermissions when the scenario asks for fewer prompts with safety intact (that's auto mode).
Choosing json output when the scenario needs live progress (that's stream-json).
Choosing a user-level file when the scenario says 'whole team'.
